name: Genistein
lead: Genistein is an isoflavone, a plant phytoestrogen found mainly in soybeans and other legumes. It was first isolated from dyer's broom (Genista tinctoria) in 1899, has the formula C15H10O5, and is the best-known isoflavone of soy foods and soy-based supplements.[1][19] People encounter it in two ways that bear on looks: as a soy-derived ingredient discussed for skin (as an antioxidant and estrogen-like plant compound) and as the compound at the centre of the long-running question in fitness circles of whether eating soy changes hormones and therefore physique.[1][20]

It binds estrogen receptors, with a stronger affinity for estrogen receptor beta than alpha in laboratory binding assays, and it inhibits tyrosine kinase enzymes in vitro.[2][3][4] Dietary interest in it spans cancer prevention, cardiovascular and bone health.[5][6]

In appearance contexts it is discussed in two ways: as a topical or oral antioxidant and phytoestrogen in skin-focused supplement and menopause marketing, and as the compound behind the long-running physique-forum question of whether soy changes male hormones, body composition or fat distribution [20][27][28]. No published trial tests genistein for wrinkles, skin ageing or other cosmetic outcomes.

Large reviews bear on the hormone question. A 2020 meta-analysis cited in Wikipedia's phytoestrogen article reported that neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals, and a 2021 review title argues that soyfoods and isoflavones do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors [31]. Wikipedia's genistein article, by contrast, lists it among endocrine-disrupting chemicals because of estrogenic activity in vitro and in vivo, citing rat studies [19]. Both positions are part of the record.

paras: Genistein was first isolated in 1899 from Genista tinctoria, which gave it its name. Its structure was established in 1926, when it was found to be identical to a compound called prunetol, and it was synthesised in 1928; a 1941 paper described genistin and its aglycone genistein from soybeans.[19] Its IUPAC name is 5,7-dihydroxy-3-(4-hydroxyphenyl)chromen-4-one, a 3-phenylchromen-4-one backbone.[1] Plants make it through the phenylpropanoid pathway, via the flavanone naringenin.[19]
Soy is the dominant source, with genistein forming roughly 40-60% of its isoflavone content; fermented foods such as miso and natto contain it too. [1]

Isoflavones also occur in lupin, fava beans, kudzu, coffee and red clover.[19] Wikipedia reports that isoflavone intake from soy may reach about 50 mg per day in Asian diets, with intake rising in Western countries alongside vegan and vegetarian diets, and that genistein is present in soy-based infant formula and in isoflavone supplements sold in some countries.[19] Genistein is also sold as an extract in supplements marketed for menopause symptoms and bone support.[20]

Soybeans are the most common dietary source, with genistein and daidzein as the main isoflavones [32]. Tofu keeps most of its isoflavones, miso has higher levels, and tempeh has the highest content among the soy foods Wikipedia lists [32]. Wikipedia's genistein article says genistein has the largest share of any isoflavone in soy protein concentrate, mature soybeans and tempeh [19].

Genistein exists in plants largely as genistin, its 7-O-glucoside, and gut microbes convert isoflavones to metabolites with possibly different estrogenic potency; blood concentrations peak about six hours after an isoflavone-containing meal [19]. Soy-based infant formula and some supplements also contain isoflavone extracts [19]. Wikipedia's isoflavone article records a 2015 EFSA risk assessment that found no adverse effects in peri- and postmenopausal women at intakes up to 150 mg per day while criticising the limited data [32].

Genistein is structurally similar to estradiol and acts on estrogen receptors alpha and beta, behaving as an agonist or antagonist depending on tissue. [1][2][7] It also inhibits tyrosine-specific protein kinases in vitro. [3] Reviews of dietary flavonoids note low oral bioavailability. [8][9] A 2007 mouse study reported that genistein in the maternal diet counteracted bisphenol A-induced changes in DNA methylation in offspring. [10]

Wikipedia says that blood concentrations peak about six hours after an isoflavone-containing meal and that gut bacteria convert genistein into metabolites with different estrogenic potency.[19] In laboratory work it is also reported to activate the G protein-coupled estrogen receptor and all three PPAR isoforms (alpha, delta, gamma), and a 1987 paper identified it as a competitive inhibitor of tyrosine kinases such as the EGF receptor.[3][19] A Molecules review describes isoflavones as among the most estrogenic plant compounds, acting with estrogenic and antiestrogenic effects depending on context.[20]

Genistein appears in cosmetic discussion because it is a phytoestrogen with antioxidant properties, and soy-isoflavone products are marketed for skin and menopause.[20][24] The pharmacology of its estrogen-receptor binding is documented, but no clinical trial of genistein on wrinkles, pigmentation or other cosmetic outcomes is available.[2][7] Wikipedia notes that the European Food Safety Authority reviewed claims in 2011-12 and found evidence insufficient for skin tone among others, and found no cause-and-effect evidence for claims such as hair growth, bone mineral density, LDL cholesterol and menopausal vascular changes.[19]

Because genistein resembles estradiol, bodybuilding and men's-health forums have debated whether soy protein and isoflavones lower testosterone, raise estrogen or soften physique. T Nation threads from 2002 onward show both camps: posters who say soy estrogen is weak and may compete with stronger estrogens at the receptor, and posters who list individual studies in support of a soy-testosterone relationship [27][28][29].

The research summary available in encyclopaedic form is that whether phytoestrogens affect male reproductive physiology remains under study; some trials found isoflavone supplements improved sperm concentration or motility, intake above typical Asian levels reportedly did not change estrogen, testosterone or semen measures, and a 2020 meta-analysis found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals [31]. Animal studies, in contrast, show estrogenic and reproductive effects at the doses used [1][19]. A 2005 randomised trial examined soy isoflavones, body composition and physical performance [21].

Wikipedia's article on genistein also notes that the soy-derived dietary forms are generally recognised as safe, while no such determination has been reported for isolated genistein [19]. Soy foods have been reported to inhibit absorption of thyroid hormone medication, and EFSA concluded in 2015 that isoflavone supplements did not affect thyroid hormone levels in postmenopausal women [33].

Grokipedia reports that older studies raised the question of soy lowering testosterone, that recent meta-analyses found no significant effect on male reproductive hormones, and that animal studies have shown reproductive effects and estrogen-dependent tumour promotion; these statements are secondary and unverified. [1] Soy intake and cancer risk has been reviewed in vitro and in vivo. [11]

Wikipedia reports that soy foods are generally recognised as safe, but that no such determination specific to isolated genistein has been reported.[19] A 2022 meta-analysis examined breast cancer risk in relation to soy and isoflavone intake in pre- and post-menopausal women, and Wikipedia cites it for preliminary evidence of lower risk.[19][22] Reviews of clinical trials of phytoestrogens, including a 2003 German review, reported no scientific evidence at the time for effects on menopausal symptoms or breast cancer risk factors but noted soy protein can lower cholesterol.[24]

The European Food Safety Authority reviewed isoflavone claims in 2011-12 and found no cause-and-effect evidence for claims including protection from oxidative damage, maintenance of LDL-cholesterol, hair growth and bone mineral density, and insufficient evidence for skin tone [19]. In the United States, isoflavones from soy have been the subject of a 1998 GRAS notification by Archer Daniels Midland [32].

Registered trials have studied genistein in heart failure, hyperlipidaemia and gut microbiota, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, colorectal and pancreatic cancer, post-myocardial infarction inflammation, paediatric obesity, and Alzheimer's disease; a 400-person trial examined vascular and bone effects in postmenopausal women. [12][13][14][15][16][17][18] No studies found on cosmetic or skin-appearance outcomes.

A 2024 double-blind placebo-controlled bicentric pilot trial in prodromal Alzheimer's disease reported that genistein was associated with cognitive preservation,[25] while a 2015 trial of soy isoflavones in Alzheimer's patients examined cognitive effects.[30] A 2004 randomised trial reported that isoflavones improved vascular reactivity in post-menopausal women with hypercholesterolaemia.[26] A 2022 meta-analysis examined isoflavones and breast cancer risk.[22]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar fitness forums, soy isoflavones are a recurring topic, framed around their estrogen-like activity and whether they affect testosterone or physique.[27][28]

claims.claim: Soy isoflavones lower testosterone and make men look softer or more feminine
claims.believers: Some forum users argue that because genistein is a phytoestrogen it can disrupt male hormones, and cite individual studies on soy and testosterone.[28][29]
claims.experts: Secondary summaries report that recent meta-analyses found no significant effect of soy on male reproductive hormones, while animal studies show estrogenic effects.[1]

claims.claim: Isoflavones are harmless or beneficial because soy estrogen is very weak
claims.believers: Other forum posts argue soy estrogen is very weak and may even reduce estrogenic effect by competing at receptors.[27][29]
claims.experts: Genistein binds estrogen receptor beta more strongly than alpha in assays and can act as an agonist or antagonist depending on tissue.[2][7]

claims.claim: Genistein supplements improve skin or hold off ageing
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and some skincare discussion frame the antioxidant and phytoestrogen activity as skin supportive.[20]
claims.experts: No published trial tests genistein for skin ageing or cosmetic outcomes; the EFSA reviewed health claims in 2011-12 and found evidence insufficient for skin tone.[19]

claims.claim: Soy is a bad protein for men because of its estrogen
claims.believers: Posters in long-running T Nation threads (2002, 2023) cite individual trials and argue that soy isoflavones can reduce testosterone or shift the hormone balance [28][29].
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia found no effect of soy or isoflavone intake on male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals [31].

claims.claim: Soy isoflavones are actually anti-estrogenic and make you more 'manly'
claims.believers: A 2002 T Nation poster argued the weak estrogen in soy binds receptors and so means less stronger estrogen [27].
claims.experts: Genistein is reported to act as an agonist or antagonist depending on tissue and binds ER beta more strongly than ER alpha in assays [2][7].

claims.believers: Posters cite its estrogenic activity and animal data when warning about soy.
claims.experts: Wikipedia classes it among endocrine-disrupting chemicals based on in vitro and rat data [19], while a 2021 review argues soy foods and isoflavones do not warrant that classification [31].

claims.claim: Soy isoflavones thin or protect the skin
claims.believers: Supplement marketing frames the antioxidant and phytoestrogen activity as skin supportive [20].
claims.experts: EFSA found insufficient evidence for skin tone [19]; no trial tests cosmetic outcomes.

claims.believers: Supplement and soy-food promotion cite lower cancer rates in soy-eating populations.
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis on breast cancer risk is cited by Wikipedia for preliminary evidence of lower risk, while rodent work reports promotion of estrogen-dependent tumours [19][22][1].

card.summary: A soy phytoestrogen studied for many conditions; no trials test it for skin or looks.

quick.overview:
Genistein is the main isoflavone in soy, a plant compound that resembles estrogen. It is sold as a supplement and studied in heart, bone and cancer research.
Its place in appearance discussions is as an antioxidant and phytoestrogen for skin; no trial of cosmetic outcomes has been found.
quick.mechanism: It binds estrogen receptors (more strongly to the beta subtype in assays) and inhibits tyrosine kinases in laboratory tests. Oral bioavailability is described as low.
quick.risks: Animal studies show estrogen-related effects; human data on hormones are reported as largely reassuring by secondary sources. It is a food component and supplement rather than an approved drug.

chain: Soy isoflavone binds estrogen receptors, mainly beta
Estrogen-like and antioxidant signalling in tissues including skin
Claimed: firmer, better-protected skin; debated: effect on male hormones and physique
angle.text: Genistein is a soy compound used in supplements and in some skincare discussion for its antioxidant and estrogen-like activity, with the idea of supporting skin quality. In gym culture it is mostly raised as a concern or a question about soy and male hormones rather than as a physique tool.
